summary: Describes a formal process for defining and standardizing new service types and their attributes for use with the service: URL scheme in the Service Location Protocol.

eli5.summary: A form that tells everyone exactly what facts to list about a new type of service, so every description looks the same.

questions: what is an slp service template
what is an abstract service type
how are slp service templates versioned
subtitle: A formal template format for describing new service types and their attributes in service: URLs.

tldr.problem: The Service Location Protocol needs a consistent way to name network services and describe their capabilities, so clients can pick the right one and tools can check registrations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the syntax of service: URLs and a text template format that lists a service type's name, version, description, URL syntax and attribute definitions. It also sets out a process for standardizing templates through a registry kept by IANA.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2609 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2165. It gives clients and administrative tools a shared, machine-readable way to understand and translate service descriptions.

facts.label: Integer range
facts.value: Signed values that fit in 32 bits

today: RFC 2609 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999. It updates RFC 2165, and the unit data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Service Templates Exist
sections.content:
RFC 2609 describes a URL scheme called service: URL, which gives network access information for a network service in a formal notation. Alongside it, the RFC defines how to describe the attributes that go with a service. Attributes let people and programs choose between services of the same type that have different capabilities.

The attributes are written in a service template, a document that both people and machines can read. The RFC lists four uses for templates: standardization (IANA archives every version once a template is standardized), service registration, client presentation of service information, and internationalization.

The service: URLs are mainly meant for the Service Location Protocol (SLP). Clients ask for services of a given type, give the attributes they want, and use the returned URL to talk to a service directly.
sections.eli5: A template is like a fill-in-the-blanks card for a type of service. Because every card has the same shape, you can compare two services and pick the one you like best.

sections.title: The service: URL Syntax
sections.content:
A service: URL must conform to an absolute URI. It has the form service: followed by a service type, a colon, and a service access point (sap). The service type is either a concrete protocol name or an abstract type followed by a URL scheme. The type is folded to lower case, so http and HTTP are the same type.

The access point starts with a site. For IP, the site begins with // and holds an optional user, a host and an optional port. The grammar also defines IPX sites (/ipx/) and AppleTalk sites (/at/). DNS host names are preferred over addresses for ease of renumbering, and a port number must be included if the protocol has no IANA assigned port number.

After the site come an optional URL path and an optional attribute list, written as semicolon-separated assignments. The path syntax is specific to each service type. An example from the RFC for an ACAP server is service:acap://some.where.net;authentication=KERBEROSV4. Attributes belong in the URL only when a client needs them to use the service. Other attributes are stored and retrieved by other means, such as SLP.
sections.eli5: A service address is a label that says what kind of service it is and where to find it. It can also carry a few notes, such as which password method to use.

sections.title: Concrete and Abstract Service Types
sections.content:
A concrete service type names a particular protocol. An abstract service type is one that a variety of different service agents can implement. Its URL includes the protocol, address and path, so the type alone does not say how to reach the service.

The RFC's example is a service that loads device drivers. Rather than writing a URL such as service:ftp:/x3.bean.org/drivers/diskdrivers.drv;driver=scsi, which it says should be avoided, the abstract type device-drivers SHOULD be used, as in service:device-drivers:ftp://x3.bean.org/drivers/diskdrivers.drv. The same service can then also be offered over tftp or http, and a search may return all of the URLs so the client can pick a protocol.

Concrete templates inherit all attributes of the abstract template they derive from, and they MUST NOT redefine them. An abstract type MUST be well specified so that programs or people have enough information to reach the service. Abstract types must not be used if a template has to work with SLPv1.
sections.eli5: An abstract type is like saying you want a pizza without saying which shop makes it. Several shops, using different ways to order, can all offer the same pizza.

sections.title: The Template Format
sections.content:
A template document starts with four identification items plus attribute definitions. The items are template-type (the service type name and optional naming authority), template-version, template-description and template-url-syntax (an ABNF for the url-path part). If no naming authority is given, it is assumed to be IANA.

A template used for standardization MUST be in English and encoded in the 0x00-0x7F subrange of UTF-8, which matches ASCII. Characters outside that range MUST be escaped, for example as \c3\a9. Items end with a blank line, and reserved characters such as ;, %, = and , MUST be escaped. Value lists are separated by commas, and a trailing comma at the end of a line continues the list onto the next line. Identifiers, type names and flags are case insensitive.

The four template items can also accompany any service registration made with SLPv2, which lets a client discover which template a service used.
sections.eli5: The template starts with a cover page that gives the name, version number, a short description and the shape of the address. After that come the details for each fact you can list.

sections.title: Defining Attributes
sections.content:
An attribute definition has up to five parts in order: an identifier, a type with flags, an optional default value list, optional descriptive text and an optional allowed-values list. Only the type is required. Each identifier must be unique within the template and is case folded.

There are five types: string, integer, boolean, opaque and keyword. Integers are limited to signed values that fit in 32 bits. A keyword attribute is defined only by its existence, so it MUST have no flags, defaults or allowed values. Booleans are single-valued only.

Four flags can follow the type: o (optional; without it the attribute is required in every registration), m (multiple values), l (literal, not to be translated) and x (clients SHOULD include this attribute in requests). If an optional attribute has an allowed-values list, it must also have a default so that the default is a member of the allowed set. Without a declared default, strings default to the empty string, integers to zero and booleans to false. Descriptive text lines start with a crosshatch character and are an integral part of the definition rather than comments.
sections.eli5: Each fact on the card has a name, a kind (words, number, yes or no), and little tags such as optional. You can also list a default answer and the only answers that are allowed.

sections.title: Versioning and Standardizing a Template
sections.content:
A new service type is proposed by submitting a template and a short description of how to use it. The template MUST start with template-version set to 0.0, and the minor number goes up once per revision. A standardized template starts at 1.0. Before 1.0 there is no guarantee of backward compatibility. Once a template reaches 1.0 its definition is frozen for that version.

After that, a new optional attribute adds one to the minor number, and old clients can still use it because they ignore attributes they do not know. Adding a required attribute, removing support for an attribute or changing a definition adds one to the major number.

Submissions are discussed on a mailing list at svrloc-list@iana.org. The IESG appoints a Designated Expert, who submits the template to IANA once it is ready. The submission has a fixed form (submitter, language, security considerations and the template text between begin and end markers), and the file is named <service-type>.<version-no>.<langtag>, such as foo.0.0.en. No template is accepted unless it includes a security considerations section and contact information for the author. IANA keeps all versions.
sections.eli5: New templates start as drafts and get better with each edit. Once everyone agrees, the template is frozen at version 1.0. Small add-ons bump the small number, and big changes bump the big number.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Translation
sections.content:
The appendix gives fictitious templates. The FOO template defines two optional, multi-valued, literal string attributes, users and groups, and has no URL path. A German copy shows how a template can be translated. Because attribute identifiers are never translated, the RFC suggests defining a localize-<tag> attribute for each tag that should be shown in another language, for example localize-users with the value Benutzer.

A second example defines an abstract Net-Transducer type with the attributes sample-units, sample-resolution and sample-rate. The concrete Net-Transducer:Thermometer adds location-description and an optional operator, and its URL path has the form ports= followed by a list of ports.

For translation, a program can convert a registration between languages if it has the template in both. Attribute identifiers, type names, flags and the constants true and false are never translated, and attributes marked literal are not translated either. Standardized types can have one master template with approved translations, and otherwise a best effort translation is used.
sections.eli5: The examples show a made-up service with two lists and a thermometer you can reach over the network. The translated card keeps the names the same but changes the words that people read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Templates are used to interpret information that SLP supplies. If templates are modified or false templates are distributed, services may fail to register correctly, or clients may be unable to interpret service information.

A service: URL names the access point and protocol, so a distributed URL could point to a service other than the one normally wanted. SLP distributes these URLs and has an authentication mechanism that allows the URLs of registered services to be signed and the signatures verified by clients. Each template also carries its own security considerations section for the specific service type.
sections.eli5: If someone hands out a fake card or a fake address, you could end up at the wrong place. Signatures help you check that an address is the real one.

viz.caption: THE SERVICE: URL GRAMMAR (ABNF EXCERPT FROM RFC 2609)

data.title: service: URL core rules
data.code:
service: URL    =   "service:" service-type ":" sap
service-type    =   abstract-type ":" url-scheme / concrete-type
abstract-type   =   type-name [ "." naming-auth ]
concrete-type   =   protocol [ "." naming-auth ]
sap             =   site [url-part]
site            =   ipsite / atsite / ipxsite
url-part        =   [ url-path ] [ attr-list ]
attr-list       =   1 * ( ";" attr-asgn )

viz.caption: ATTRIBUTE FLAGS DEFINED BY THE TEMPLATE FORMAT

items.label: Optional
items.desc: The attribute is optional; without this flag it is required in every registration.

items.label: Multiple
items.desc: The attribute can take several values of the declared type; not allowed for booleans.

items.label: Literal
items.desc: Not meant to be translated into other languages.

items.label: Include in requests
items.desc: Clients SHOULD include this attribute when asking for services.

viz.caption: HOW A TEMPLATE VERSION NUMBER CHANGES

cells: Starts at 0.0; minor number goes up once per revision
Minor number goes up by one
New required attribute, removed attribute or changed definition
Major number goes up by one
